title: The battle of prayer (CCC 2725–2745)
hookLine: distraction, dryness, lack of faith, and not giving up

cards: "Pray without ceasing." Three words in Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians. Then the actual attempt.
A quiet room, eyes closed, the first line of a prayer. Within a few breaths, a grocery list arrives. Then an email that needs answering.
Then an old argument, replayed with a better comeback. Minutes later, the prayer is still on its first line. It would be easy to decide you're bad at praying, and stop.
Back on day twenty, Teresa of Avila admitted prayer went that way for her for years. The Catechism has a word for it, and it isn't failure. Today: the battle of prayer.

teach.b: The Catechism says it plainly: prayer is a battle. Not against God, but against ourselves, our surroundings, and, in its words, the wiles of the tempter. It isn't a sign something's broken; it's what praying is like.
Then it names the troubles. Distraction first, and the advice is surprising: don't hunt distractions down. Chasing them is falling into their trap.
Just turn back to the heart, and notice what the distraction shows you, because it shows what you're attached to. The grocery list isn't the enemy. It's information.
Next, dryness: prayer with no taste at all, no feeling, no words.

The Catechism calls this a moment of sheer faith, staying with Jesus in his agony and in the tomb, and reaches for his own image: "unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die," it remains alone.
Something is happening under the soil. Then lack of faith, which shows up less as open doubt than in what we put first, when other cares that seem urgent crowd ahead of prayer.

And acedia, a listless weariness about spiritual things. The answer to all of it is the same: persevere. Luke introduces one of Jesus's stories this way: "that we ought always to pray, and not to faint."
A widow keeps coming back to an unjust judge until he finally gives her justice. The point isn't that God is like that judge. The point is the widow.

how: Catholics who struggle with distraction or dryness in prayer are usually encouraged by priests and spiritual directors to keep a regular time of prayer anyway, gently returning to it each time the mind wanders.

games.q: what does “the battle of prayer” mean?
o: the struggle to keep praying through distraction
an argument with God until he finally gives in
a war fought by Catholics in defense of the faith

s: the Catechism says to hunt down every distraction
it says hunting them down falls into their trap; turn back to the heart instead.
the Catechism calls prayer a battle
against ourselves, our surroundings and the wiles of the tempter.

games.q: you're the widow in Jesus's story. the judge doesn't fear God or respect anyone, and he's turned you away. what do you do?
games.why: she keeps coming back until he gives her justice. Luke says Jesus told it so that we "ought always to pray, and not to faint."

practice: If you pray, choose one short line, the first words of the Our Father or just the name of Jesus; if you don't, choose your breath, and rest on it.
When your mind wanders, don't scold it: name where it went in one word, list, worry, plan, and come back. Each return is the practice, not a failure of it.

wordCard.voice: The battle of prayer. In the Catechism, the struggle with distraction, dryness, lack of faith and weariness, met by humble watchfulness and perseverance.

orig.note: Greek: without ceasing, unceasingly — the word in "pray without ceasing," 1 Thessalonians 5:17.

carryVoice: Your line: keep coming back. Every single return counts, even the hundredth. Same time tomorrow.
